newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela ends Zaire talks, declares progress.
newsitem.headline: Mandela ends Zaire talks, declares progress.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela, taking centre stage in peace efforts, said on Thursday progress had been made in his separate talks with Zaire's warring parties, but kept the details to himself.
Mandela met Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba for an hour in Pretoria on Thursday.
On Wednesday he held talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila in attempts to get the two sides in roundtable talks and hopefully broker a truce.
"All I want to say is that there is progress which is encouraging," Mandela told a news conference after Thursday's talks, the contents of which were kept confidential.
A veil of secrecy shrouded the rivals' talks with Africa's most respected leader, whose 10-day absence on a trip to Asia from Friday dampened hopes of rapid success.
Foreign ministry officials said the statements made at the news conferences after Mandela's two sets of talks would be the only public comment for now about the tricky negotiations.
Aviation sources said Kabila, who arrived quietly in South Africa on Tuesday, was hoping to fly out on Friday.
His forces have overrun a 1,000 km (600-mile) stretch of Zaire since they took up arms in October against the ailing Mobutu, a veteran leader they call a despot.

A regional military source said the rebels were besieging the eastern Zairean town and transport hub of Kindu but appear to be holding off attacking the heavily fortified base to allow as many civilians as possible to leave. Morale among government troops was said to be low and panic had set in among them.
In a strong position, Kabila is keen on direct talks.
"Let's hope the negotiations will start soon," Kabila said after meeting Mandela, but added he saw little hope of a swift truce.
Mobutu has so far refused talks, a stance Mandela hopes to soften.
"Mr Ngbanda appreciates the importance of peace in Zaire and that this peace will only be brought about by negotiations with Laurent Kabila," the South African president said.
Asked if direct talks were now a possibility, Ngbanda said only: "That is part of our discussions."
He said he had met U.S. officials and that Mobutu was committed to a peaceful settlement, but one that must "respect Zaire's territorial sovereignty".
Zaire, which has employed foreign mercenaries to bolster its army, accuses Uganda and Tutsi-led Rwanda and Burundi of fighting with the rebels, many of whom are also ethnic Tutsis.
Zaire's three eastern neighbours deny involvement in the conflict, which has sent tens of thousands of local people and Hutu refugees fleeing from Rwanda and Burundi.
African leaders agreed on Wednesday to hold a crisis summit on March 18 and 19. Mandela has said he wants to meet Mobutu, who has been treated in Europe for cancer, at the same time.
A spokesman said Mandela, whose peace efforts have U.N., U.S. and African support, wanted "to say encouraging words to both sides", but not to enter into any sort of negotiations.
The United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity have, with scant success, been leading efforts to bring peace to Zaire and its eastern neighbours in the Great Lakes region.
Mandela until recently eschewed calls from other Africans to employ his moral stature, and South Africa's regional muscle, to help solve the continent's troubles.

His office denies any change of heart but foreign affairs analysts say Mandela has either decided to put African stability at the heart of his strategy, or has looked fearfully at Zaire's rapid disintegration and realised no one else could now help.
